title: Run Dart In VS Code
text:
1. Install Dart SDK (if no Flutter)

Download from dart.dev.
Add the bin folder of the SDK to your system PATH so your terminal knows what dart means.



2. Use Dart bundled with Flutter (if Flutter is installed)

Flutter includes its own Dart SDK inside:
<flutter_installation_directory>\bin\cache\dart-sdk
The easy route: add this to your PATH instead:
<flutter_installation_directory>\bin
That way, both Flutter and Dart commands just work.
Verify with:
dart --version



3. Set up VS Code

Open VS Code.
Install the Dart extension from the marketplace (search “Dart” by Dart Code).

If you’ll be doing Flutter, install Flutter extension too.

Open a folder where your project will live.



4. Create a Dart project or file

Run in terminal:
dart create my_project
Or just make a file called main.dart with something trivial:
void main() {
  print('Dart is alive inside VS Code.');
}



5. Run Dart code

From the integrated terminal:
dart run main.dart
Or use the Run ▶ button in VS Code’s editor if the extension is installed.


Recommendation: If you already have Flutter, don’t install Dart separately—just use Flutter’s bundled SDK. Next step: Add <flutter>\bin to PATH, install the Dart extension in VS Code, and test with a simple main.dart.

title: Input Output
text:
The Dart language comes with sound null safety.
Null safety prevents errors that result from unintentional access of variables set to null. For example, if a method expects an integer but receives null, your app causes a runtime error. This type of error, a null dereference error, can be difficult to debug.
With sound null safety variables are ‘non-nullable’ by default: They can be assigned only values of the declared type (e.g. int i=42), and never be assigned null. You can specify that a type of a variable is nullable (e.g. int? i), and only then can they contain either a null or a value of the defined type.
Sound null safety changes potential runtime errors into edit-time analysis errors, by flagging when any non-nullable variable hasn’t been initialized with a non-null value or is being assigned a null. This allows you to fix these errors before deploying your app.
https://dart.dev/null-safety







Warning



In Dart 2.x SDKs, you can enable or disable sound null safety through configuration of the project SDK constraint. To learn more, see Enabling/disabling null safety.
Dart 3–planned for a mid-2023 release– will require sound null safety. It will prevent code from running without it. All existing code must be migrated to sound null safety to be compatible with Dart 3. To learn more, see the Dart 3 sound null safety tracking issue.

section: Why a Stateful Widget needs a State class
text:
Why a Stateful Widget needs a State class
A StatefulWidget is split into two parts:

The widget class

Immutable.
Holds configuration data (like constructor parameters).
Exists only to tell Flutter: “Here is how my UI should be built.”

The State class

Mutable.
Holds the data that can change over time.
Provides the logic for updating the UI.
Calls setState() to tell Flutter to rebuild the widget tree.




Why not just put everything in one class?
Flutter’s UI system is built around immutability:

All widgets in Flutter are immutable (their fields cannot change once created).
When something changes, Flutter doesn’t “mutate” the widget — it rebuilds a new widget tree.

If StatefulWidget itself were mutable, it would break this consistency. By separating configuration (StatefulWidget) from behavior (State), Flutter achieves:

Performance efficiency: only the State object is preserved during rebuilds, not the whole widget.
Clarity: you can see which parts are static (the widget class) and which parts are dynamic (the state).
Reusability: the same widget class can be paired with different states in different contexts.




How it works in practice
When Flutter rebuilds:

The old State object is kept.
The new StatefulWidget object is created (with new config data if needed).
The existing State is reattached to this new widget.

That’s why you must inherit from State — so Flutter knows:

where to store your mutable data, and
how to rebuild your widget when that data changes.




In short:
A StatefulWidget is immutable by design. Its mutable companion, the State class, exists to hold data and logic that can change. That’s why every StatefulWidget must be paired with a State subclass.

Homepage Widget:

It has a list called _movies to store the data fetched from the JSON file.

Loading JSON Data:

It uses setState() to refresh the UI, displaying the loaded movies and hiding the “Load Data” button.

User Interface:

text:
1. Application architecture
Mobile applications frequently need to manage more than simple settings. An animal shelter, for example, needs to maintain records of animals entering its care, photograph those animals, document their adoption, and retain historical information. Such an application combines structured database records with files stored on the device.
This chapter develops a Humane Society Pet Tracker, a complete Flutter application that integrates SQLite, the device camera, the photo library, and a responsive user interface. It builds on familiarity with Dart classes, asynchronous programming, forms, navigation, and StatefulWidget.
The application supports animal intake, editing, photography, adoption information, archiving, and permanent record deletion. Each animal appears as a card in a grid. Selecting a card opens an editing form; the floating action button opens an empty intake form.
Four components cooperate to provide this functionality:
The database and file system serve different purposes. SQLite stores structured information such as names, dates, and adoption status. The file system stores photographs. A database field named imagePath connects each record to its photograph.
This separation allows the application to query animal records without retrieving large binary photographs in every database result. SQLite can store binary data using the BLOB storage class, and doing so is appropriate in some applications. For this project, separate files simplify image display and keep ordinary record queries small. The trade-off is that the application must manage the relationship between files and records.

Platform configuration
On Android, image_picker normally uses the system camera and photo selection interfaces without additional manifest configuration. If your application independently declares camera permission, it must also handle the applicable permission requirements; do not add permissions merely to troubleshoot an unrelated camera error.
On iOS, open ios/Runner/Info.plist and include these entries within the existing top-level <dict>:

The Pet class represents a row in the pets table. Its nullable id distinguishes a new object, whose identifier has not yet been assigned by SQLite, from an existing record.

SQLite does not have a separate Boolean storage class. The example represents Boolean status using integers. Dates are stored as text in YYYY-MM-DD format; the sample permits manual entry and does not enforce date validity. Approximate age is also text, making values such as 6 months easy to enter but less convenient for numeric sorting.

Mapping objects to database rows
The toMap() method converts a Dart object into a Map<String, dynamic> whose keys match the database columns. The Pet.fromMap() factory constructor performs the reverse operation. This mapping keeps SQL-related details separate from the widgets that display animal information.

4. Database operations and archiving
DatabaseHelper uses the singleton pattern to provide a shared helper instance. Its database getter opens the database when needed and retains the resulting handle. The onCreate callback creates the table when a new database is initialized. The database version is set to 1; future schema changes would require a migration strategy.
CRUD describes the four fundamental database operations:



Operation
Method
Result




Create
insertPet()
Adds an animal record.


Read
getPets()
Retrieves active or archived records.


Update
updatePet()
Modifies an existing record.


Delete
deletePet()
Permanently removes a database row.



The read operation uses a parameterized filter:
where: 'isArchived = ?',
whereArgs: [showArchived ? 1 : 0],
orderBy: 'id DESC',
The placeholder ? is supplied through whereArgs rather than constructing SQL through string concatenation. The query returns the selected status group, with the highest identifiers first.
Archiving is an update, not a deletion. Setting isArchived to 1 removes an animal from the active view while retaining its information. An archived record can be opened and restored by turning off its archive switch and saving it again. The permanent delete operation, by contrast, removes the row after confirmation.

The form uses a GlobalKey<FormState> to validate input, TextEditingController objects to manage editable text, a dropdown to select the animal category, date pickers to populate date fields, and a switch to control archived status. The same form supports creation and editing: a null pet argument represents a new intake, while an existing Pet supplies initial values.
When saving, the form validates the required name, constructs a Pet object, chooses insertion or update, and returns to the grid using Navigator.pop(). The grid then queries SQLite again to reflect the changes.

8. Understanding the application lifecycle
WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized() initializes Flutter’s bindings before the application starts. The grid loads database records through initState() and displays a progress indicator during the asynchronous query. Each time the archive filter changes or a form closes, _refreshPets() retrieves records and calls setState() to rebuild the interface.
The form initializes controllers using either existing values or defaults. When the form is removed, dispose() releases those controllers. The save method awaits the database operation before leaving the screen, and the mounted check prevents navigation through a disposed widget in that method.
The photograph is copied when selected, before the animal record is saved. This means canceling a form, replacing a photograph, or deleting a database row can leave an unused image file behind. The sample deliberately does not implement file cleanup. In addition, some asynchronous callbacks lack mounted checks, and database and picker failures do not yet have comprehensive error handling. These are useful areas for extending the implementation.

10. Design limitations and production considerations
This application illustrates local CRUD and device integration rather than a complete shelter management system. A production application would need stronger validation, error handling, safe file cleanup, database migrations, and a backup strategy. Absolute image paths can become invalid if the application storage location changes; storing relative file identifiers and resolving them against the current documents directory is another design option.
Adopter names and addresses are personal information. A real deployment should consider access controls, encryption where appropriate, retention policies, and secure backups. Ordinary local SQLite storage alone does not provide these safeguards.

A data model maps Dart objects to database rows, a database helper encapsulates CRUD operations, and Flutter widgets display and edit the records. By combining image_picker, path_provider, sqflite, and responsive layouts, the application demonstrates how several independent Flutter capabilities can be integrated into a single working design.

Application state and persistent storage
Applications often need to remember user preferences between sessions. A settings screen, for example, is of little value if the user must select a theme and enter a name every time the application starts. This chapter introduces persistent key-value storage in Flutter through a working settings application. It also explores how to customize the installed application name and launcher icon.
Familiarity with Dart, StatefulWidget, setState(), TextField, Future, and basic Flutter layouts is assumed.
When a user enables dark mode, the application is expected to remember that choice the next time it opens.
A Flutter StatefulWidget can remember a value while the widget is alive. But a normal variable is not automatically saved when the operating system terminates the application. Calling setState() redraws the interface; it does not save a value to disk.
You will give your application a small amount of memory:
You will change each setting, fully close the application, reopen it, and check whether your selections are restored.

title: Flutter: Shared Preferences and Persistent Settings
text:
Shared preferences and key-value pairs
The shared_preferences plugin provides simple, platform-backed key-value storage. We give each value a key (a string identifying it) and store a supported value under that key.



Key
Type
Example value




display_name
String
Alex


dark_mode
bool
true


font_size
double
22.0



The package supports int, double, bool, String, and List<String>. A read of an absent key produces null, so we supply defaults using the ?? operator:
final String name = await prefs.getString('display_name') ?? '';
final bool dark = await prefs.getBool('dark_mode') ?? false;
final double size = await prefs.getDouble('font_size') ?? 18.0;
Why SharedPreferencesAsync? Current package guidance recommends SharedPreferencesAsync or SharedPreferencesWithCache for new work. SharedPreferencesAsync performs asynchronous reads against platform storage instead of relying on a local cache. It works with Future and await and avoids cache-staleness surprises. The older SharedPreferences.getInstance() API still appears in many online examples, but it is designated legacy in the current documentation.
Limitations: This is suitable for small, noncritical preferences, not a relational database, large datasets, passwords, access tokens, or financial/medical records. It is not an encrypted secrets store. The plugin documentation also warns that disk persistence is asynchronous and not guaranteed to complete before abrupt termination, even after the write call returns. Do not treat it as transactional durable storage.
Connection to SQLite: SQLite stores structured records that can be queried. Shared preferences store a few named values. Use the simplest tool that fits the data.

text:
Test persistence

Run the app and enter a name. Select Save Name.
Turn Dark mode on.
Move the slider to a different font size and release it.
Fully terminate the running application, then launch it again. A Flutter hot reload alone is not a persistence test.
Confirm the name, dark mode, and font size have been restored.
Press Restore Defaults, restart again, and confirm the original values return.

Expected results: The name persists after saving; the theme persists after toggling; font size persists after releasing the slider; and reset removes the three saved entries.

Troubleshooting

Import not found: Check that you ran flutter pub add shared_preferences inside the correct project directory. Try flutter pub get.
Changes disappear: Make sure you saved the name, released the slider, and fully restarted the app rather than only running a hot reload. Check the debug output for storage exceptions.
Preferences seem to vanish after reinstalling: Application storage may be removed on uninstall or app-data clearing; do not treat local preferences as an account backup.
App will not build: Check flutter --version, flutter doctor, and the package’s SDK constraints. A newly published package version may require a newer Flutter SDK; flutter pub add normally resolves a compatible release.
Preference read produces an error: Verify that a given key is always used with the same data type. For example, do not write an int under font_size and then attempt to read it with getDouble().

text:
Customizing the application name and launcher icon
An application has several distinct identifiers and visual elements that determine how it appears inside Flutter and on the device launcher:








Item
Where it appears
How to change it




App-bar title
At the top of the Flutter screen
AppBar(title: ...) in main.dart


Flutter application title
Used by Flutter/platform integrations; not necessarily the launcher label
MaterialApp(title: ...) in main.dart


Installed app name / launcher label
Under the app icon on the device home screen and in the app list
Android manifest or iOS Info.plist


Launcher icon
Home screen / application launcher
Platform icon resources, conveniently generated with flutter_launcher_icons



Important: Changing MaterialApp.title does not by itself change the name printed beneath the installed app’s icon. Likewise, changing Icon(Icons.settings) inside the UI does not change the launcher icon.

Step 1 — Choose an application name
Use My Settings or choose another appropriate short name. Short names are less likely to be truncated on mobile home screens.
In lib/main.dart, find the MaterialApp constructor and change its title property:
MaterialApp(
  title: 'My Settings',
  // Keep the rest of your existing properties.
)
Do not replace the whole MaterialApp from the earlier exercise with only this snippet; change the existing property and retain its theme, darkTheme, home, and other settings. Similarly, locate the existing AppBar and change its title to const Text('My Settings') if you want the visible heading to match.


Step 2 — Change the installed application name on Android
Open:
android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
Inside the existing <application> element, find the android:label attribute. Change only its value:
<application
    android:label="My Settings"
    android:name="${applicationName}"
    android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher">
    <!-- Keep the application's existing activity and other configuration. -->
</application>
This is an illustrative excerpt, not a replacement for your entire manifest. Keep all generated <activity>, <meta-data>, and other entries. The ${applicationName} placeholder is part of the generated Flutter Android project and should remain unchanged.
The launcher label is separate from the Android application ID (such as com.example.persistent_settings_demo). Changing the launcher label does not require changing the application ID.


Step 3 — Change the installed application name on iOS
Open:
ios/Runner/Info.plist
Inside the top-level <dict>, locate the CFBundleDisplayName entry and set it to:
<key>CFBundleDisplayName</key>
<string>My Settings</string>
If the key is absent, add this pair inside the main <dict>. Preserve the other entries. CFBundleDisplayName controls the name shown beneath the app icon on iOS. Do not confuse it with the bundle identifier, which is a separate setting.
Platform note: Building for iOS normally requires macOS and Xcode. If you use Windows, complete and test the Android portion; you can still inspect the iOS configuration file if your project contains it.


Step 4 — Prepare a launcher icon image
Create a square PNG image, preferably 1024 × 1024 pixels. Use an original simple design: for example, a gear or slider symbol for this settings application. Keep the essential artwork away from the edges because mobile launchers may mask or crop icons into different shapes. For the basic iOS icon, use an opaque background rather than transparency.
Create these folders in the Flutter project:
persistent_settings_demo/
├── assets/
│   └── icon/
│       └── app_icon.png
├── android/
├── ios/
├── lib/
│   └── main.dart
└── pubspec.yaml
Place the image at assets/icon/app_icon.png. The generator reads this file directly; it does not need a Flutter assets: declaration in pubspec.yaml merely to create launcher icons.


Step 5 — Install the launcher-icon generator
From the project root, run:
flutter pub add --dev flutter_launcher_icons
This adds the tool under dev_dependencies in pubspec.yaml, separate from the shared_preferences runtime dependency. This package is used during development to generate native icon files; the app does not call it from main.dart.


Step 6 — Configure the icon generator
Create a file in the project root named flutter_launcher_icons.yaml (at the same level as pubspec.yaml):
flutter_launcher_icons:
  android: true
  ios: true
  image_path: "assets/icon/app_icon.png"
  remove_alpha_ios: true
This is the documented configuration format for the flutter_launcher_icons package. android: true and ios: true replace the respective default launcher icon assets; remove_alpha_ios helps generate an iOS-compatible opaque icon.
For this introductory exercise, a single source image is sufficient. Production Android applications may additionally benefit from separately designed adaptive icon foreground and background layers and an optional monochrome variant for themed icons.


Step 7 — Generate the icon files
In the project root, execute:
flutter pub get
dart run flutter_launcher_icons
The generator writes platform-specific sizes and resources, rather than using the 1024-pixel source file as-is on every device.
Typical generated locations include:

Android: android/app/src/main/res/mipmap-*/ and other icon resources as appropriate.
iOS: ios/Runner/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset/.

Do not manually rename the files the generator produces without also updating the platform configuration.


Step 8 — Rebuild and verify
Stop the running app and run:
flutter clean
flutter pub get
flutter run
flutter clean is a troubleshooting precaution rather than a requirement for every icon change. Hot reload does not reliably update installed launcher icons or platform manifest metadata; you need a new native build and installation.
Return to the device’s home screen or app drawer and confirm:

The app name below the icon is My Settings.
The icon displays your new artwork instead of Flutter’s default icon.
Opening the app still shows the saved display name, dark-mode setting, and font size after a normal restart.

If the old icon remains, first ensure the icon generation command succeeded and the image path is correct. Then rebuild; if the launcher is caching the old icon, uninstall and reinstall the app only after checking any data you need to preserve, because uninstalling normally removes the app’s locally stored shared preferences.


Common errors







Symptom
Likely cause / correction




File not found from the generator
Check that assets/icon/app_icon.png exists and the YAML path matches exactly.


Default icon remains
Re-run dart run flutter_launcher_icons, stop the app, and rebuild rather than hot reload.


Name changes inside the app, but not below the icon
Update android:label or CFBundleDisplayName; MaterialApp.title alone is insufficient.


iOS icon shows unexpected transparency/background
Use an opaque square icon and remove_alpha_ios: true.


Settings disappear after testing
Uninstalling/reinstalling can remove the app’s stored preferences. Test persistence by closing and reopening the installed app without uninstalling it.

title: SQFLITE
text:
Program Summary
This Flutter application demonstrates how to integrate the Sqflite package to manage data locally on a device. It lets the user add, edit, delete, and view car records—each with a make, model, year, and color. Data is stored persistently in a SQLite database using the CarDatabase helper class. The app’s interface features a simple form at the top for input and a scrollable ListView below that displays all saved cars. Each entry includes buttons to edit or delete a record. This project teaches CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations, asynchronous database handling, and dynamic UI updates in Flutter.
